clue.text: One hopes he's the one down!

definitions.text: One hopes he's the one down!

blocks.clueFragment: One hopes he's the one down!
blocks.note: surface reading: a hopeful person wishing someone else to be the one feeling low
setter's reading: in a contest you want your rival to be the one knocked down or beaten

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is itself a Down entry, so 'the one down' playfully points at the grid too; the real sense is the rival you hope gets floored.
explanation.definitionFit: The person on the other side of a game or fight is exactly the one you hope will lose.

clue.text: An inclination to use jargon

blocks.note: first meaning: a slope or tilt
second meaning: the special talk of a trade or group

explanation.surface: Someone has a habit of slipping into technical buzzwords.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a sloping tilt and the private vocabulary of a particular group or trade.

clue.text: Stretch of water to divide the North

blocks.note: to sever is to cut apart
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A body of water forming a boundary that splits off the northern region.
explanation.walkthrough: The Severn is Britain's longest river, flowing from Wales into the Bristol Channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is a long stretch of flowing water, and this one is a famous British example.

clue.text: Austere person is kind of acid about society

indicators.note: one thing placed about another surrounds it on both sides

blocks.note: acetic acid is the acid in vinegar
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A severe, self-denying person is sour and cutting about high society.
explanation.walkthrough: The acid's letters split after their first letter to hold the society abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lives a strictly self-disciplined life, denying themselves comforts, is austere.

clue.text: Harsh stones near the churchyard

indicators.note: things placed near each other sit side by side, so the pieces are joined in sequence

blocks.note: scree is a mass of loose stones on a slope
split in two: CH is the abbreviation for church and Y for yard

explanation.surface: Rough stones lying beside a graveyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Churchyard' must be split into its two halves, each abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: A screechy sound is shrill and grating, so it is harsh on the ear.

clue.text: Ropes giving support to suitable possessions

indicators.note: in a Down entry the supporting part sits underneath, so it follows the other piece

blocks.note: proper means fitting or suitable
ropes tie things, and ties are cords

explanation.surface: Ropes are holding up a load of appropriate belongings.
explanation.definitionFit: Properties are things a person owns, such as houses or land, so they are possessions.

clue.text: Some paper used in study

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are wanted, a run inside them

blocks.note: the run starts inside the first word and ends inside the second

explanation.surface: A scrap of paper has been put to use in somebody's study room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' looks like the room, but it is the verb meaning to read carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse something is to read or examine it closely, which is a way to study it.

clue.text: The orator's awkward situation in the Park

definitions.text: The orator's awkward situation in the Park

blocks.note: surface reading: a public speaker who has got into a tight spot
setter's reading: the famous spot in London's Hyde Park where anyone may stand up and speak

explanation.walkthrough: Being in a corner is being in an awkward situation, but here it is the open-air place in Hyde Park, London, set aside for public speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hyde Park spot belongs to orators, and its second word also means a tight predicament.

clue.text: Swallow hurriedly in the bar

blocks.note: first meaning: gulp food down fast
second meaning: a sliding metal rod that fastens a door

explanation.surface: Someone gulps a drink down fast in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub; it is the fastening rod on a door.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to gulp food quickly and a sliding rod used to fasten a door.

clue.text: Team matter about learner in the test

indicators.note: one thing placed about another surrounds it on both sides

blocks.note: a cricket or football side has eleven players
pus is the matter discharged from a wound
L is the learner plate on a British car

explanation.surface: A team's business concerns a beginner sitting an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: The eleven-plus was a British exam taken at about age eleven deciding entry to grammar school.
explanation.definitionFit: It was an examination sat by schoolchildren, so it is a kind of test.

clue.text: Complain about head, doctor being brought in

indicators.note: something brought in ends up inside another thing

blocks.note: bean is slang for the head
MO is a medical officer

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about their boss once a doctor is called in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' reads as a boss, but here it is the slang word for the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: To bemoan something is to lament or grumble over it, which is to complain about it.

clue.text: Cancel change to a better oil

indicators.note: to change the letters is to make them into a different order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Scrap the plan and switch to a superior grade of oil.
explanation.definitionFit: To obliterate something is to wipe it out entirely, as when a mark is struck through and cancelled.

clue.text: It's experienced in coagulated milk, they say

indicators.note: what they say is heard spoken rather than read

blocks.note: curd is milk that has set into lumps, so this is being inside curd

explanation.surface: Something gets stuck in milk that has gone lumpy, people report.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a cost or loss is to suffer or undergo it, so it has been experienced.

clue.text: This is the flattest beer in two ways

indicators.note: one item set in another goes inside it

blocks.note: ST, short for street, is a way; two of them
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: This pint is the most lifeless beer, whichever way you look at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In two ways' sounds like 'in two senses', but it means the beer sits between two streets.
explanation.definitionFit: Stale drink has lost its fizz, so the most stale beer is the least lively, or flattest.

clue.text: Those officiating care for parking in stages

indicators.note: one thing given for another takes its place, as a swap

blocks.note: steps are stages in a process
P is the sign for parking
a ward is someone in another's care, and ward also means guardianship

explanation.surface: Race officials look after the parking arrangements in stages.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'care for parking in stages' as: put the word for care in place of the parking letter within the word for stages.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewards are the officials who run and supervise events such as race meetings.

clue.text: Signary used in the plant

indicators.note: letters that are used or worked over are altered from their original order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A set of signs is employed within the plant.
explanation.walkthrough: A signary is a set of written symbols, such as an alphabet; the word is chosen for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Syringa is the botanical genus of lilacs, and the name is also used for mock orange, both flowering shrubs.

clue.text: The spirit of sportsmen?

blocks.note: surface reading: the sporting character shown by athletes
setter's reading: being game, ready and plucky, as hunters and players are, with a nod to game as sport

explanation.walkthrough: Game means both a sport and plucky willingness, so the quality fits sportsmen twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: Being game means being keen and brave, so the noun names a plucky, willing spirit.

clue.text: Lady Heather, in the main very sentimental

indicators.note: in the main means mostly, so most but not all of the word is kept

blocks.note: Maud is a woman's name, famous from Tennyson's poem
ling is common heather

explanation.surface: A woman named Heather becomes tearful while out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a second name, but it is the plant; 'the main' is not the sea but 'mostly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Maudlin means tearfully or gushingly emotional, which is excessively sentimental.

clue.text: The AA man in trouble? I don't like it

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disarray, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A motorist sees the breakdown patrolman in difficulty and is unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: The AA is the British Automobile Association, whose patrolmen rescue broken-down cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Something anathema to you is a thing you loathe, so it is what prompts the complaint quoted.

clue.text: Joint flat, we hear, is required

indicators.note: what we hear is taken by sound, not spelling

blocks.note: the knee is a joint, and dead means flat or lifeless

explanation.surface: A worn-out knee is reported to need attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Something needed is necessary, which is what is meant by its being required.

clue.text: Man to look around for an opening word

indicators.note: looking around something surrounds it on all sides

blocks.note: to see is to look
Sam is a man's name

explanation.surface: A fellow glances about searching for something to say first.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Arabian Nights tale, 'open sesame' is Ali Baba's password that opens the robbers' cave.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the magic password that makes the cave door open, so literally a word for opening.

clue.text: Assembly's thrash held up in cathedral city

indicators.note: in a Down entry, lifting a word up makes it read from bottom to top
one item set in another goes inside it

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
a see is a bishop's seat, the city with his cathedral

explanation.surface: A council's beating is delayed in a city with a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held up' looks like 'delayed', but in a Down clue it means the word is flipped upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A senate is a governing or legislative body, a formal assembly of members.

clue.text: Erred and began to go wrong in the drinking place

indicators.note: letters that go wrong fall out of their proper order

blocks.note: the letters of both words, without the joining word, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone made mistakes and slipped up while out at the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an outdoor area of a pub where people sit and drink, so it is a place for drinking.

clue.text: The garden trowel produces a hollow

indicators.note: the words produce the target from within themselves, holding it ready-made

blocks.note: the run starts at the end of the first word and ends at the start of the second

explanation.surface: Digging with a small garden tool leaves a small hole in the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' is part of the surface only; the letters come from the end of one word and start of the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A dent is a small depression in a surface, which is a slight hollow.

clue.text: River race

blocks.note: first meaning: a river in Devon, England
second meaning: to dash or move swiftly

explanation.walkthrough: 'River race' suggests a rowing event; the words are separate meanings, the Devon river and the verb to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a river flowing through Dartmoor in Devon and also means to dash suddenly.

clue.text: Personal involvement in an item of clothing?

definitions.text: Personal involvement in an item of clothing?

blocks.note: setter's reading: a personal stake in how something turns out
surface reading: being keen on a garment such as an undershirt

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for a personal stake is read literally as concern for a vest, a sleeveless undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a personal stake in an outcome stands to gain from it, which is the standard idiom.
